title: Undoing things safely
objective: By the end of this lesson you can undo any of the four common mistakes deliberately, and you know which undos are safe on shared work and which ones rewrite history.

blocks.text: Most fear of Git is fear of doing something irreversible. Almost nothing is. The reason people panic is that the undo commands have unhelpful names and the internet answers every question with the most destructive one. Four situations cover nearly everything.
Situation 1: I edited a file and want it back

blocks.caption: Throw away uncommitted changes to a file
lines: git restore app.py            # discard unstaged edits — back to whatever is STAGED
#                               (with nothing staged, that is the last commit)
git restore .                 # every unstaged edit — no undo for this one

blocks.title: This one is genuinely irreversible
blocks.text: Uncommitted work has never been recorded anywhere, so discarding it is the one Git operation with nothing to recover from. Run git diff first and look at what you are about to throw away.
Situation 2: I staged something I did not mean to

blocks.caption: Unstage without losing the edit
lines: git restore --staged app.py   # remove from the staging area, keep the changes
git status                    # it is back to 'not staged'

blocks.text: Situation 3: my last commit was wrong

blocks.caption: Amend — replace the most recent commit
lines: git commit --amend -m "A message that is actually correct"
git commit --amend --no-edit   # fold this into the last commit, keep its message

blocks.title: Amend rewrites — only before anyone else has it
blocks.text: Amending replaces the previous commit with a new one that has a different identity. On work only you have, that is tidy. On a commit you have already pushed and someone else has pulled, it forces everyone into a conflicting history. The rule for the whole lesson: rewriting is fine before sharing, and a problem after.
Situation 4: a commit further back was wrong

blocks.caption: Revert — undo by adding a new commit
lines: git log --oneline                 # find the bad commit
git revert a3f91c2                # create a commit that undoes exactly that one

blocks.text: Revert is the safe undo: it changes nothing that already exists, it adds. Anyone who already has the history keeps it intact and simply receives one more commit. This is the correct tool for undoing anything that has been shared.
The one to understand before you use it: reset

blocks.title: --hard is the command people regret
blocks.text: It discards the commit and your working changes together. Committed work can usually still be recovered through the reflog, which the next module covers — but uncommitted work cannot. Before any reset --hard, ask what is in the working directory that has never been committed.

rows: Yes — this is the shared-work answer

blocks.title: Perform each undo once
steps: Run: echo 'oops' >> notes.txt && git add notes.txt
Run: git restore --staged notes.txt (unstaged, edit still there)
Run: echo 'a real edit' >> notes.txt && git commit -am "Wrong message"
Run: git commit --amend -m "Corrected message" && git log --oneline -3
Run: git revert --no-edit HEAD && git log --oneline -3
blocks.expected: An edit discarded, a file unstaged, a message corrected in place, and finally an undo that appears as its own commit — which is the difference between rewriting the past and adding to it.

cheatsheet: git restore <file> — discard unstaged edits, back to the staged version (irreversible: look with git diff first)
git restore --staged <file> — unstage but keep the edit
git commit --amend — replace the last commit (only before pushing)
git commit --amend --no-edit — fold a forgotten file into the last commit
git revert <id> — undo by adding a new commit; safe on shared work
git reset --soft HEAD~1 — drop the commit, keep changes staged
git reset --hard HEAD~1 — drop the commit AND the changes
Rewriting is fine before sharing and a problem after
Uncommitted work is the only thing Git genuinely cannot recover

checkpoint.prompt: A bad commit was pushed three days ago and colleagues have pulled it. How do you undo it?

choices.A: git reset --hard to before it, then force push
choices.B: git revert <id>, which adds a commit undoing that change

checkpoint.explanation: Revert changes nothing that already exists — everyone keeps their history and simply receives one more commit. Rewriting shared history forces conflicts on everyone who has it.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the difference between git reset --soft HEAD~1 and git reset --hard HEAD~1 ?

choices.A: --soft only works on the first commit
choices.B: --soft removes the commit but keeps your changes staged

checkpoint.explanation: --hard removes the commit and discards the changes from disk. Both drop the commit. The difference is what happens to the content — and --hard is the one that takes your working changes with it.

checkpoint.prompt: Which operation can Git genuinely not recover from?

choices.A: Discarding uncommitted changes with git restore

checkpoint.explanation: Work that was never committed was never recorded anywhere, so there is nothing to recover. Everything already committed leaves a trace that can usually be found again.

checkpoint.prompt: You forgot to include one file in the commit you just made, and have not pushed. What is the tidiest fix?

choices.B: Make a second commit called 'fix previous commit'
choices.D: git revert HEAD then commit everything again

checkpoint.explanation: Amend folds the forgotten file into the existing commit and keeps its message. It is safe here precisely because the commit has not been shared yet.
